analysis.one_liner: Creates public financing for congressional elections and overhauls presidential public financing to boost small donors and curb lobbyist money.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees for the entire two-year Congress after 30 members signed on in support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rebuilt the presidential public financing system so small donations are matched five-to-one, and created a new public financing program for House and Senate campaigns. Candidates who joined would get public money in exchange for accepting lower contribution limits, refusing money bundled by lobbyists, and limiting personal spending. It also raised the voluntary $3 tax check-off that funds the system to $20, tightened disclosure of coordinated spending, and barred candidates from raising money for super PACs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters gain a funded alternative to big-donor campaign finance: candidates who can gather 400 small in-state contributions of $250 or less would qualify for five-to-one public matching funds, up to $2 million for a House race and $10 million for a Senate race [S2][S3]. That would let people without access to wealthy networks run for office, and would reduce the pressure on winning officeholders to spend their time courting large donors and lobbyists. Voters also gain from the bill's tightened disclosure of coordinated spending and its ban on candidates soliciting funds for super PACs [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates public financing for congressional elections: candidates who collect at least 400 in-state contributions of $250 or less qualify for a five-to-one match, up to $2 million for House candidates and $10 million for Senate candidates [S2][S3].

Raises the presidential primary match from one-to-one to five-to-one for small donations and repeals spending limits that had made the old public financing system unattractive, while barring participating candidates from taking lobbyist-bundled money or PAC money [S2][S3].

Raises the voluntary taxpayer check-off that funds public financing from $3 to $20 per return ($6 to $40 joint), with inflation indexing, and requires tax software to present the check-off neutrally rather than pre-answering it [S2][S3].

Tightens the definition of coordinated spending so outside groups working with campaigns count as contributions, clarifies that candidates and officeholders cannot solicit or direct funds to super PACs, bans candidate joint fundraising committees with outside political committees, and expands disclosure of lobbyist-bundled contributions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large donors, lobbyists who bundle checks, and super PAC fundraising operations would have less leverage over participating candidates. Taxpayers fund the system, but only through the voluntary check-off — the bill raises that check-off from $3 to $20 per return and lets taxpayers donate additional amounts directly, and the first cycle is covered by repayable Treasury advances [S2][S3]. Participating candidates accept lower contribution limits and a $50,000 cap on personal spending in exchange for the public funds [S3].

drawbacks.text: The program is funded by taxpayers: the bill raises the check-off from $3 to $20 and authorizes Treasury advances for the first cycle, so the public financing pool must be large enough to cover many simultaneous campaigns — a real cost and a real risk of underfunding if too few taxpayers opt in [S3].

Participation is voluntary, so a candidate facing an opponent who declines the program and keeps unlimited big-donor and super PAC fundraising still faces the old money race; repealing the old expenditure limits without a constitutional fix for independent spending leaves outside spending untouched [S2][S3].

Public money going to political candidates is contested on principle — critics argue taxpayers should not finance campaigns for candidates they oppose, and the bill repeals public financing for party conventions while allowing individual contributions of up to $25,000 per cycle for conventions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is public money for private leverage: participating candidates trade a portion of big-donor fundraising for a five-to-one match on small donations, paid for by a voluntary check-off rather than general tax dollars. The honest design questions are whether the check-off raises enough money and whether voluntary participation can overcome the incentive to take unrestricted money in a system where outside spending remains unlimited. But as a template for shifting campaign funding toward small donors and away from lobbyists and super PACs, the bill is coherent and its costs to the public are limited and self-selected.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever acted on it; no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no action of any kind for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. David Price introduced the Empowering Citizens Act on January 15, 2013, with 11 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the Committee on House Administration and to the Ways and Means Committee, in each case only for the provisions under their jurisdiction [S1].
Thirty members cosponsored the bill, 29 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
The action record shows no activity after the referral — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent lawmakers and the large donors, lobbyist bundlers, and super PAC operators who fund campaigns are better off: the existing fundraising system, in which members of Congress must constantly court big money, continued unchanged for the 2014 elections and beyond.

for.name: Rep. David E. Price
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled an original cosponsor group of a dozen members.

for.name: 30 cosponsors (29 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of public financing for congressional campaigns and the other reforms.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, leaving it to die without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 Democratic cosponsors were joined by exactly one Republican, and the committees that buried the bill were run by the Republican majority; support was heavily but not entirely Democratic.

industries.note: The bill bars participating candidates from accepting contributions bundled by registered lobbyists and expands disclosure of lobbyist bundling, cutting off a core way influence is purchased. Lobbyists would lose access-for-dollars leverage over publicly funded candidates.

industries.industry: Super PACs and large political donors
industries.note: The bill clarifies that candidates and officeholders cannot solicit, direct, or transfer funds to super PACs, bans candidate joint fundraising committees with outside committees, and treats coordinated spending as a contribution. Candidates taking public funds would no longer need to be part of the big-money machinery.

industries.industry: Professional political consultants and campaign vendors
industries.note: Stricter coordination rules would limit consultants from serving outside groups and campaigns simultaneously, but publicly funded campaigns still hire consultants and buy advertising. The super PAC fundraising side of the business would shrink.

The bill raises the limit on coordinated party spending for presidential races and lets parties spend unlimited small-dollar money for participating candidates, but repeals public financing of national conventions, bans soft money for conventions, and restricts candidate fundraising for party committees.

The bill requires Treasury regulations ensuring tax software does not automatically accept or decline the public financing check-off, a light-touch rule aimed at keeping the voluntary fund solvent without dictating business practices.
